name: Boztepe and the Ordu Cable Car
desc: A 550-metre hill straight behind the city, reached by a four-minute gondola from the seafront. The summit itself is just tea terraces and a car park, but the view down the curve of the bay — hazelnut slopes one side, cargo cranes the other — is why Ordu built the thing. Sunset fills it with local families rather than tourists.
season: May–Oct for clear air; the gondola stops in strong wind, which is common Nov–Feb
tip: Ride up before sunset and walk the forest road back down to the harbour in about 45 minutes instead of paying for the return leg.
rev: Nearly everyone rates the view and the cheap ride, then complains about weekend queues at the lower station, closures in wind or fog, and a summit that has been paved over with cafés.
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 25 km west into Ordu; the lower station is a 10-minute walk from the seafront

name: Perşembe Plateau
desc: An unusually flat grass plateau at 1,800 m above Aybastı, ringed by low ridges and dotted with stone-and-timber yayla houses. Cloud pours in from the coast most afternoons and swallows the whole plain in twenty minutes. In July the kemençe and the tulum come out for the festival and the meadow fills with cars.
season: Jun–Sep only; the access road is snow-blocked roughly Nov–May and fog can sit for days
tip: Come the week before the July şenlik — same wildflowers, same butter, none of the twenty thousand people.
todo: Walk the flat meadow to the ridge
Buy yayla butter and tulum cheese
rev: Visitors call the light and the silence worth the climb, but warn about the festival weekend crush, near-zero visibility in fog, almost no accommodation, and shepherd dogs that take their job seriously.
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 100 km inland via Aybastı; the last 20 km is paved but narrow and steep

name: Çambaşı Plateau
desc: A broad spruce-fringed plateau at 1,850 m in Kabadüz, with a small ski centre of two lifts and a handful of hotels. In winter the snow is deep and dry and the queues are nonexistent; in summer the same slopes are cattle pasture and the road is lined with people selling honey out of car boots.
season: Jan–Mar for snow, Jun–Sep for the pasture; April and November are mud and closed lifts
tip: The ski centre only guarantees weekend lift operation outside school holidays — phone the hotel before driving up midweek.
todo: Two-lift ski day with no queues
rev: People praise the empty pistes and the price, then note the tiny ski area, patchy lift operation midweek, thin après-ski, and a summit road that ices badly after dark.
entry: Free to enter; ski lift pass ≈₺400 (€8.50) a day
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 55 km south via Kabadüz on a fully paved mountain road; winter tyres essential

name: Ulugöl
desc: A small landslide lake at 1,100 m in the hills above Gölköy, black-green under alder and hornbeam, with a level path all the way round in half an hour. There are rowing boats, a few wooden picnic decks and a trout restaurant. Mist comes off the water at dawn and burns away by nine.
season: May–Oct; the lake often freezes over Jan–Feb and the road ices
tip: Walk the far shore where the boardwalk ends — the picnic crowd never gets past the boat jetty.
todo: Rowing boat before the wind picks up
rev: Locals rate it as a cheap easy day out; the standard complaints are weekend picnic litter, loud music from the car park, and a narrow approach road that is genuinely awkward for a wide vehicle.
entry: ≈₺60 (€1.30) per car at the nature park gate
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 75 km inland via Gölköy; last 12 km narrow and paved

name: Jason Cape
desc: A blunt green headland west of Perşembe where the old coast road still runs, with a small 1868 Greek church on the tip and shingle coves on both flanks. Argonaut legend gets attached to it, deservedly or not. The sea here is clear enough to swim and there is no hotel strip, only fishing boats and a tea garden.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; autumn storms hit this cape hard
tip: Take the old coastal road from Perşembe rather than the new dual carriageway — the tunnels bypass the cape entirely and you will miss the turning.
rev: Reviewers love the setting and the free access, but say the church is usually locked, the coves get windy fast, and summer weekends bring picnickers who leave the shingle a mess.
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 40 km west; leave the D010 at Perşembe and follow the old shore road

name: Aybastı
desc: A highland market town at 900 m where the hazelnut country ends and the pasture begins, and the gateway to Perşembe Yaylası. The Thursday market brings down cheese, butter and beans from the yaylas, and half the shops still sell scythes and cowbells. Nobody comes here for sights; they come for the road above it.
season: May–Oct; the town works year-round but the plateau road above closes with snow
tip: Time your visit for the Thursday pazar and buy the yayla butter there rather than from the roadside stalls higher up, which charge triple.
todo: Kabak tatlısı at a town fırın
Drive on up to Perşembe Yaylası
rev: Travellers describe an unpretentious working town with genuinely good dairy and no tourist infrastructure at all — no proper hotel, limited evening food, and everything shut by nine.
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 90 km inland; regular minibuses run from Ordu and Fatsa otogar

name: Giresun Island
desc: The only real island in the eastern Black Sea, a 40,000 m² lump of rock and scrub two kilometres offshore, carrying a ruined Byzantine wall, a chapel and the so-called Hamza Taşı. Ancient writers made it the Amazons' island of Ares. On 20 May the whole city sails out for the Aksu festival and circles the rock three times.
season: May–Sep for boats; nothing runs in a swell, which means most of Nov–Mar
tip: Outside the 20 May festival you need to hire a fishing boat from the harbour yourself — there is no scheduled service, and the crossing is cancelled the moment the wind turns.
rev: The setting and the legend win people over; the recurring gripes are unreliable boats, no facilities whatever on the island, overgrown paths, and a landing that is impossible in any sea at all.
entry: Free to land; boat hire from Giresun harbour ≈₺500–800 (€11–17) per boat
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 45 km east to Giresun; boats leave from the town harbour

name: Kümbet Plateau
desc: A 1,650 m plateau in Dereli that is really a small summer village — wooden houses, a mosque, a church-shaped chapel and a permanent row of tea houses. It is the easiest of the Giresun yaylas to reach and the busiest, with a July festival that closes the road. Beyond the last house the pasture runs empty for kilometres.
season: Jun–Sep; road usually snowbound Dec–Apr
tip: Push another 8 km past the village towards Karagöl for the views everyone photographs and thinks they took at Kümbet.
todo: Walk out past the last yayla house
rev: Visitors find it green, cool and easy to reach, then complain that it has become a car park with cafés, that fog cancels the view without warning, and that festival weekends are gridlock.
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 60 km south of Giresun via Dereli; paved the whole way, minibuses in summer

name: Bektaş Plateau
desc: Higher, barer and far quieter than Kümbet, at around 2,100 m on the Giresun mountain ridge, with a scatter of huts and horses grazing among rock outcrops. Above the tree line the cloud sits below you most mornings. The onward track towards Şebinkarahisar over the ridge is one of the best rough drives in the region.
season: Late Jun–mid Sep; snow lingers into June and returns in October
tip: The ridge track south to Karagöl and Şebinkarahisar needs high clearance and is nothing to attempt in fog — turn back if the cloud drops below the huts.
rev: People rate the emptiness and the light highly; the complaints are a rough final stretch of road, only basic bungalow accommodation, no phone signal, and cold nights even in August.
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 80 km south from Giresun via Dereli; the last 15 km is gravel

name: Mavi Göl
desc: A small landslide-dammed lake on the Dereli road, sitting in a steep spruce gorge with drowned tree trunks still standing in the shallows. The colour swings from turquoise to slate depending on rain and light, and it is at its best when the water is low enough to expose the pale stone shoreline.
season: May–Oct; heavy spring rain turns the water brown and muddy
tip: Stop on the way up to Kümbet rather than on the way down — morning light hits the water, and by afternoon the gorge is in shadow.
todo: Shoreline walk to the drowned trees
Photograph the gorge from the road above
rev: A quick and genuinely pretty roadside stop, though visitors note that the colour depends entirely on recent rain, the shore is littered, and there is nowhere safe to park more than two cars.
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 45 km south of Giresun on the Dereli–Kümbet road

name: Şebinkarahisar Castle
desc: A fortress welded onto a black volcanic plug 1,300 m above an inland plain, three hours from the sea and in a completely different climate. Walls, cisterns and a rock-cut stair survive; the summit is a knife edge with a 300-metre drop on the town side. Below it the Meryem Ana monastery clings to another cliff.
season: May–Oct; the plateau is cold and often snowy Dec–Mar
tip: Drive to the upper car park then take the stepped path — the older track from the town centre is a punishing 45-minute climb in full sun.
todo: Meryem Ana monastery below the cliff
rev: Visitors call it the most dramatic castle site in the region and are surprised how empty it is; the complaints are unprotected drops, patchy restoration, and a long 110 km drive from the coast on a slow road.
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 110 km inland from Giresun over the mountains — about 2.5 hours by car or bus

name: Kulakkaya Plateau
desc: A 1,500 m plateau above Bulancak, close enough to the coast that on a clear evening you can see the Black Sea from the meadow. Spruce forest, a couple of hotels and a paraglider launch that catches thermals off the ridge. It is the yayla people from Giresun drive up to for supper and drive home from the same night.
season: Jun–Sep for the meadow; some winter weekends work for snow when the road is cleared
tip: Book a table at a plateau restaurant for the hour before sunset — the sea view only appears when the afternoon haze drops.
todo: Sea view from the meadow edge
rev: Praised as an easy escape from the coastal heat with real food and a rare sea view, but people warn of fog closing in for days, weekend crowds from Giresun, and hotel prices that spike in August.
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 30 km east to Bulancak and 25 km up a paved mountain road

name: Tirebolu
desc: A small port between two bays with a Genoese-era castle, St Jean, on the headland dividing them and a row of old timber houses behind the quay. Hazelnut sacks stack on the pavement in August. It is the one town on this coast where the dual carriageway did not obliterate the waterfront.
season: Jun–Sep for the sea; the town is pleasant year-round but wet
tip: Walk out to St Jean castle at dusk — the gate is unlocked and the two bays light up on either side of you.
todo: St Jean castle on the headland
Old timber houses behind the quay
rev: Travellers like the relaxed harbour and cheap fish; the usual gripes are the highway noise behind the town, a small stony beach, and a castle that is little more than walls with no signage.
onward: Ordu–Giresun (OGU) airport, then 85 km east on the coast road; every Trabzon–Giresun bus stops here

name: Sümela Monastery
desc: A Greek Orthodox monastery glued to a sheer cliff 300 m above the Altındere valley, founded in the fourth century and rebuilt in stages until 1923. The painted rock chapel is the point: layers of frescoes inside and out, badly vandalised, still extraordinary. From the valley floor it looks impossible, which is exactly the intended effect.
season: May–Oct; sections close after rockfall and the valley road can shut in winter
tip: Take the first shuttle of the day from the lower car park — by eleven the cliff stair is a single-file queue and the chapel interior is unphotographable.
todo: Valley view from the cliff terrace
rev: Almost everyone calls it worth the trip, then reports long shuttle queues, restoration scaffolding, parts of the complex roped off, and disappointment that the famous outer fresco wall is only partly accessible.
entry: ≈₺700 (€15) for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 50 km south via Maçka to the Altındere car park, and a compulsory minibus shuttle up the valley

name: Uzungöl
desc: A landslide lake at 1,100 m under steep spruce ridges, with a wooden mosque on the shore that appears on every poster of the Black Sea. It is also the most heavily developed spot in the region: hotels stacked up both valley walls, jet skis on the water, and Gulf-market restaurants everywhere. The surrounding yaylas are the redeeming part.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; July–Aug is peak Gulf season and fully booked
tip: Sleep in Uzungöl but spend the day up at Demirkapı or Şekersu yayla — the lake itself is worth about ninety minutes.
todo: Trout grilled at a valley lokanta
rev: Opinion splits sharply: the setting is genuinely beautiful, but reviewers repeatedly describe overbuilding, traffic jams on the single valley road, inflated food prices and constant construction noise.
entry: Free; ≈₺60 (€1.30) vehicle fee at the valley barrier
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 100 km east and inland via Of and Çaykara; minibuses run from Trabzon in summer

name: Hagia Sophia of Trabzon
desc: A thirteenth-century Komnenian church on a bluff above the sea, with the finest surviving Byzantine frescoes on this coast and a carved stone frieze of Adam and Eve over the south porch. It has been a working mosque again since 2013, so much of the painted interior now sits behind curtains and false ceilings.
season: Year-round; closed to visitors during the five daily prayers
tip: Go mid-morning between prayers and ask the görevli about the narthex — the best frescoes are in the porch, outside the curtained prayer hall.
todo: South porch relief of Adam and Eve
rev: Visitors call the architecture and the surviving paintings remarkable, but consistently express frustration that the reconversion to a mosque hides most of the frescoes and that photography inside is restricted.
entry: Free — it functions as a mosque; dress modestly and remove shoes
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 8 km west along the shore; city buses and dolmuş marked Ayasofya run from Meydan

name: Atatürk Mansion, Trabzon
desc: A white neo-baroque villa of 1903, built by a Greek banking family and given to Atatürk by the city; he stayed three times and drafted part of his will here in 1937. The rooms are preserved with his furniture and books, and the terraced garden of magnolia and cedar looks straight down over Trabzon to the sea.
season: Year-round; the garden is best May–Jun when the magnolias are out
tip: The garden is the real attraction and is free to walk in — you only pay if you go inside the house.
todo: City and sea view from the lawn
rev: Turkish visitors treat it as a pilgrimage and rate it highly; foreign visitors more often find the interior modest, the labelling Turkish-only, and the hillside approach hard to reach without a taxi.
entry: ≈₺60 (€1.30) — municipal museum, not covered by the Museum Pass
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 6 km up into Soğuksu; a dolmuş marked Köşk runs from Meydan, or a short taxi

name: Zigana Pass
desc: The 2,030 m saddle where the ancient Trabzon–Erzurum caravan road crosses the Pontic wall — the point where Xenophon's men are supposed to have seen the sea. Spruce and cloud on the north side, bare brown steppe on the south, within twenty minutes of driving. The 14.5 km tunnel below now takes all the lorries.
season: Jun–Oct for the old pass road; snow closes it frequently Nov–Apr while the tunnel stays open
tip: Skip the tunnel and take the old road over the top — that is where the climate flips and where the roadside honey and kuymak stalls still are.
todo: Watch the forest give way to steppe
rev: Drivers rate the scenery and the sudden climate change, but warn about fog, black ice, lorry traffic on the tunnel approaches, and a summit that in bad weather offers nothing but grey.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 65 km south on the D885 towards Gümüşhane; every Trabzon–Erzurum bus crosses it, now by tunnel

name: Çal Cave
desc: A wet, cold river cave in the hills above Düzköy, with about a kilometre lit and walkable of a system that runs far deeper. Water runs through the whole length, there are small lakes and a constant drip, and the air stays around 6 °C. It is a genuine caving experience rather than a floodlit corridor.
season: Year-round inside; the approach road is awkward in snow Dec–Mar
tip: Wear proper shoes and take a jacket — the floor is running water and people turn back at the first pool in sandals.
todo: Walk the lit gallery to the far lake
Yayla road up to Karadağ afterwards
rev: People are impressed by the scale and the running water, and equally consistent about the cold, the constant dripping that ruins cameras, slippery steps, and a long narrow road up from the coast.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 45 km west and inland via Düzköy; car or taxi only, no public transport to the cave

name: Hıdırnebi Plateau
desc: A 1,600 m ridge-top pasture above Akçaabat, close enough to the coast that the cloud sea below you is sitting on Trabzon. Timber houses, a small mosque and a July festival with tulum and horon that draws the whole district. Most days a bank of white fog rolls up the valley by mid-afternoon and swallows everything.
season: Jun–Sep; road usually closed by snow Dec–Apr
tip: Stay the night in a plateau pansiyon — the cloud inversion happens at dawn and day-trippers from Trabzon always miss it.
rev: Visitors describe the cloud-sea mornings as the best thing in the province and then list the drawbacks: a steep narrow road, very basic rooms, no food after dark, and fog that can cancel the whole point.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 15 km west to Akçaabat and 30 km up a paved but tight mountain road

name: Vazelon Monastery
desc: The other cliff monastery of Maçka, dedicated to St John, older than Sümela and left almost entirely alone. Roofless halls, a fresco of the Last Judgement fading on an outer wall, hazel and ivy growing through the floors. There is no ticket office, no shuttle and usually nobody else at all.
season: May–Oct; the forest track is impassable after heavy rain and in snow
tip: The last two kilometres are a rough forest track — leave the car at the village of Kiremitli and walk up in about forty minutes.
todo: Last Judgement fresco on the outer wall
Walk up through the hazel woods
rev: Those who make it call it more atmospheric than Sümela precisely because it is empty; the complaints are the unsigned rough track, structural collapse, graffiti from treasure hunters, and no facilities whatsoever.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 45 km south via Maçka; turn off at Kiremitli — a high-clearance car or a walk from the village

name: Akçaabat
desc: A coastal town west of Trabzon with two separate reasons to stop: Ortamahalle, a hillside quarter of restored nineteenth-century timber-and-stone houses looking over the sea, and the köfte, which is a national brand. The old quarter is small enough to walk in an hour and has a Byzantine church at the top of it.
season: Year-round; May–Oct for the terraces, though it rains in every month
tip: Eat the köfte at a grill in the town centre, not on the Ortamahalle terraces — same meat, half the price, and the local queue tells you which one.
todo: St Michael church at the top of the quarter
rev: The köfte lives up to its reputation for most people; the recurring complaints are that Ortamahalle is small and partly derelict, parking is hopeless, and the restored houses are mostly closed cafés.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 15 km west on the coast road; constant dolmuş from Trabzon Meydan

name: Sultan Murat Plateau
desc: A wide pasture at 2,100 m above Çaykara, named for the Ottoman sultan who camped here and marked by a memorial to the Turkish soldiers who died on this ridge in 1916. Above the last houses the grass runs to bare rock and small tarns. It is the highest road-accessible yayla in Trabzon and it feels it.
season: Late Jun–Sep; snow blocks the road roughly Nov–May
tip: Combine it with Uzungöl in one loop rather than backtracking — the link road over the ridge is rough but passable in a normal car in summer.
todo: Night sky above the tree line
rev: Reported as spectacular and near-empty, with the standard caveats: a long climb on broken asphalt, no shops, cold even in August, and the monument area busy on national commemoration days.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 95 km east via Of and Çaykara, then 25 km of steep mountain road

name: Ayder Plateau
desc: The famous hot-spring yayla at 1,350 m at the head of the Fırtına valley, with waterfalls dropping straight into the settlement and the Kaçkar trailheads starting behind it. It has been ruined and half-repaired by concrete building; a long demolition and regeneration programme has been tearing out illegal hotels for years. The valley above is still superb.
season: Jun–Sep; snowbound and mostly shut Dec–Apr, and it rains in every month
tip: Use Ayder as a bed and start walking at dawn towards Huser or Aşağı Kavrun — the settlement itself empties of interest by mid-morning.
todo: Walk up to Aşağı Kavrun yayla
rev: Everyone agrees the setting is exceptional and the building is not: reviews repeatedly cite concrete hotels, ongoing demolition works, mud, day-tripper coach crowds and inflated prices in August.
entry: Free to enter; ≈₺75 (€1.60) vehicle fee at the barrier, thermal baths extra
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 70 km east and inland via Ardeşen and Çamlıhemşin; minibuses run from Ardeşen and Pazar

name: Kaçkar Mountains National Park
desc: Türkiye's only genuinely alpine range outside the far east: glaciated granite to 3,937 m, permanent snowfields, tarns, and a wall of rain forest on the northern flank. Brown bear and chamois are present and occasionally seen. The classic crossing from Ayder over the Çaymakçur pass down to Yusufeli takes three or four days.
season: Mid-Jul–mid Sep for the high passes; snow lies on them until July and returns in October
tip: Hire a local guide in Ayder or Olgunlar for the crossing — the cloud sits on the ridges most afternoons and the cairned routes vanish completely.
todo: Deniz Gölü tarn below the summit
rev: Trekkers rate it among the best walking in the country, while warning about persistent afternoon cloud and rain, unmarked routes, aggressive shepherd dogs, and very basic hut accommodation.
entry: Free on foot; vehicle fees at some valley barriers
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport for the north side via Çamlıhemşin, or Erzurum (ERZ) and Yusufeli for the south; no public transport above the last villages

name: Pokut Plateau
desc: A line of cantilevered timber Hemşin houses on a 2,000 m spur, standing above a valley that fills with cloud most evenings so the huts appear to float. The walk on to Sal and Hazindak along the ridge takes two easy hours. It is the image most people have in mind when they say they want to see the Kaçkars.
season: Late Jun–Sep; the track is snow-covered and impassable Nov–May
tip: The last 10 km from Şalpazarı junction is a rutted dirt road best done in a hired 4x4 or the local minibus — ordinary hire cars regularly ground out and get stuck.
todo: Ridge walk on to Sal yayla
Sunset cloud inversion from the huts
Sleep in a restored Hemşin house
rev: Widely described as the best view in the region, with equally consistent warnings: a punishing dirt access road, rooms that must be booked weeks ahead in August, cold nights, and fog that hides everything for days.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then Ardeşen and Çamlıhemşin, then 20 km of mountain track — 4x4, local minibus or a two-hour walk up

name: Sal Plateau
desc: Pokut's quieter neighbour, an hour's walk along the same ridge, with fewer houses, more grazing cattle and an open view down the Fırtına valley towards the sea. Because almost everyone stops at Pokut for the photograph, Sal keeps its working-yayla character: milk churns, cut hay, and dogs that bark at strangers.
season: Late Jun–Sep; deep snow Nov–May
tip: Walk the ridge from Pokut to Sal in the late afternoon and have someone bring your bag round by track — it is the best hour of light and a genuinely easy path.
todo: Fresh milk and muhlama at a hut
Look down the whole Fırtına valley
rev: Walkers prefer it to Pokut for the quiet and the food, but note there is hardly any organised accommodation, no shop, unreliable phone signal, and the same rough access track.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then Çamlıhemşin and the Pokut track; most people walk the last hour from Pokut

name: Gito Plateau
desc: A grass shoulder at 2,100 m on the far side of the valley from Pokut, reached by a switchback track from Ayder side. Fewer houses, more open meadow, and a horizon of Kaçkar peaks that stays visible longer in the day because the cloud comes up the other valley first. Horses graze loose across the whole plateau.
season: Jul–Sep; snow closes the track Nov–Jun
tip: Gito clears earlier in the morning than Pokut — if you have one dawn and the forecast is bad, come here.
todo: Loose horses on the open meadow
rev: Reported as emptier and more open than Pokut with equally good views, though visitors flag a steep unmade track, a couple of very simple guesthouses, and rain that can set in for a week.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then Çamlıhemşin and a 4x4 track from the Ayder road; local jeep transfers can be arranged in Ayder

name: Zilkale
desc: A medieval tower castle on a spur 750 m above the Fırtına river, built to watch the caravan route to the Kaçkar passes and now standing in wet forest with cloud tearing past the keep. The interior is small — a chapel, cisterns, a stair to the tower — but the position is the whole point.
season: May–Oct; the valley road can be closed by landslip after heavy rain, and snow shuts it in winter
tip: Photograph it from the road bend about 500 m below rather than from inside — the classic shot of the castle on its spur cannot be taken from the castle.
todo: Continue up to Çat and Elevit
rev: Consistently rated for atmosphere and the drive in; complaints are a narrow cliff-edge road with no barrier, a small interior that takes fifteen minutes, and mist that hides it entirely on many days.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then Ardeşen, Çamlıhemşin and 15 km up the Fırtına valley road; a car is essential

name: Fırtına Valley and its Arch Bridges
desc: Forty kilometres of gorge running from the sea at Ardeşen up into the Kaçkars, with the fastest river in the country at the bottom of it and a series of high single-arch stone bridges — Şenyuva, Çatal, Mikron — thrown across it in Ottoman times. Tea and hazelnut give way to spruce, then to bare rock.
season: May–Oct; peak snowmelt in May makes the river spectacular and rafting serious
tip: Stop at the Şenyuva bridge and walk across it rather than photographing from the car — from the far bank the whole gorge opens up behind it.
todo: Drive on to Zilkale and Çat
rev: Praised as one of the great valley drives in Türkiye, with recurring complaints about hydroelectric construction scarring the riverbed, landslip closures, a very narrow road, and rain that can last a week.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 50 km east to Ardeşen and inland via Çamlıhemşin; minibuses reach Çamlıhemşin, a car beyond it

name: Palovit Waterfall
desc: A wide fifteen-metre curtain of water dropping over a mossy shelf in the forest above Ayder, reached by a rough track and then a ten-minute walk. Spray keeps everything within thirty metres soaked and green. Hydro schemes elsewhere in the valley have taken water off other falls; this one still runs hard.
season: May–Jul at full snowmelt volume; low and disappointing by late September
tip: Go in the morning — the gorge is in deep shade from early afternoon and the fall is unphotographable after about two o'clock.
rev: Visitors find it genuinely powerful in early summer and reduced to a trickle in autumn, and repeatedly warn about a badly rutted access track, slippery steps and no facilities at the parking spot.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then Çamlıhemşin and the Ayder–Elevit valley road; the last few kilometres need clearance

name: The Tea Terraces of Çayeli
desc: The hills behind Çayeli are terraced with tea from the shoreline to about 800 m, a corrugated green that changes tone three times a day with the light and the rain. Between May and October pickers work the slopes with shears and sacks, and the factories along the coast road run around the clock.
season: May–Oct during the three picking rounds; the bushes are dull and bare-looking Dec–Mar
tip: Ask at a village tea house whether you can walk a row with a picker — most say yes, and it is the only way to understand how steep the ground actually is.
todo: Walk a picking row with a grower
Village tea house above the terraces
Watch the fresh leaf go into a factory
rev: People find the landscape more striking than expected and the growers welcoming; the complaints are almost no signage or organised visits, factories that turn away drop-ins, and constant drizzle.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 25 km west to Çayeli; take any village road inland from the coast highway

name: Rize Ziraat Botanic Garden
desc: A terraced garden on the hill directly above Rize, laid out on the old tea research station: camellia, rhododendron, kiwi and magnolia stepped down the slope with the port and the sea below. The wooden tea house at the top is where the city goes to sit, and the tea is grown fifty metres away.
season: Apr–Jun for the camellias and rhododendrons; open and pleasant year-round
tip: Walk up from the city rather than taking a taxi to the top — the path enters through the lower terraces, which is where the planting is best.
todo: Tea at the hilltop wooden pavilion
Port and sea view at dusk
rev: Locals rate it as the best free thing in Rize; visitors note that the tea house gets packed on weekend afternoons, the labelling is thin, and the whole place is exposed to the constant rain.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 35 km west into Rize; the garden is a 20-minute walk or short taxi up from the centre

name: Çamlıhemşin
desc: The last real town in the Fırtına valley and the hinge for everything above it: Zilkale, Ayder, Pokut, the Kaçkar trailheads. Hemşin is spoken in the shops, the women wear the black-and-yellow puşi headscarf, and the bakery does a cornbread worth stopping for. Old stone-and-timber houses stand along the river below the road.
season: May–Oct; the town stays open in winter but the roads above it do not
tip: Buy your food here — Ayder and the yaylas above have almost nothing, and prices double for every kilometre of altitude.
todo: Hire a jeep for the yayla tracks
rev: Treated by most travellers as a supply stop rather than a destination, and praised for exactly that — though people note the town itself is small, parking is tight, and the through traffic to Ayder never stops.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 50 km east to Ardeşen and 20 km inland; frequent minibuses from Ardeşen and Pazar

name: Anzer Plateau
desc: A remote 2,000 m plateau in İkizdere whose meadows carry an unusual density of flowering herbs, which is why the honey made here sells for more than any other in the country. The village is small and the hives are everywhere. Genuine Anzer honey is scarce, certified, and widely counterfeited on the road below.
season: Jul–Sep, and the flowering peak is late July; the road is closed by snow Nov–Jun
tip: Buy only from a producer in the village with the cooperative's certificate — anything sold as Anzer honey on the coast road is almost certainly not.
todo: Buy certified honey from a hive owner
rev: Those who make the drive rate the meadows and the honey highly; the standard complaints are a long rough climb, a very short season, no accommodation, and rampant fake honey everywhere below the plateau.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 60 km via İkizdere and a further 25 km of steep mountain road; car only

name: Karagöl-Sahara National Park
desc: Two separate pieces above Şavşat: a small black lake trapped in spruce forest at 1,500 m, and the Sahara yayla, a broad flower meadow higher up. The forest here is old, wet and dense, the sort where you hear woodpeckers and see nothing. Georgia is twenty kilometres away over the ridge.
season: Jun–Sep; the park roads are snowbound Nov–May
tip: The Karagöl lake and Sahara yayla are 25 km apart on different roads — do not assume one visit covers both, and do Karagöl first thing before the picnic parties arrive.
rev: Visitors describe genuinely primeval forest and quiet lakes, then complain about picnic litter at Karagöl on summer weekends, a rough forest road, and very limited food or accommodation nearby.
entry: ≈₺80 (€1.70) per vehicle at the park gate
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 130 km via Artvin to Şavşat, then 25 km on forest roads; car essential

name: Borçka Karagöl
desc: A landslide lake at 1,450 m in deep forest above Borçka, with a boardwalk around the shore and the reflection of the surrounding beech and spruce that made it famous. In late October the whole bowl turns copper. The last stretch of road is 25 km of climbing on a mostly unsurfaced surface.
season: Late Oct for colour, Jun–Sep for the forest; snow closes the road Dec–Apr
tip: Arrive before nine — the water only mirrors the trees while the air is still, and by mid-morning the breeze and the coaches both arrive.
todo: Full boardwalk circuit at first light
Autumn reflection from the north shore
rev: Widely rated for the autumn reflections, and just as widely criticised for a rough 25 km climb, crowds and drone noise on October weekends, litter, and overpriced bungalows booked out months ahead.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 90 km east via Hopa to Borçka, then 25 km of mountain road

name: Camili (Macahel) Biosphere Reserve
desc: Six villages in a valley that drains north into Georgia, cut off from the rest of Türkiye by a 1,800 m pass — the country's first UNESCO-recognised biosphere reserve, with primary forest that has never been logged and the protected Caucasian honeybee. Hay is still cut by scythe and stacked on wooden frames.
season: Jun–Sep; the Çavuşlar pass is snow-blocked roughly Nov–May and the valley is then reachable only through Georgia
tip: You need your passport even though you never leave Türkiye — there is a jandarma checkpoint at the pass because the valley sits inside the border zone.
rev: Visitors describe an intact traditional landscape and outstanding honey, and warn about the exposed unpaved pass road, the border checkpoint, homestay-only accommodation, and no mobile signal in most of the valley.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then Hopa and Borçka, then 40 km over the Çavuşlar pass on a partly unsurfaced road; 4x4 preferable

name: Kafkasör Plateau
desc: A pine-shaded plateau at 1,300 m eight kilometres above Artvin, best known for the bull-wrestling festival in the last week of June, where paired bulls push each other around a natural arena until one walks away. Outside the festival it is a quiet forest picnic ground with a long view down the Çoruh gorge.
season: Late Jun for the festival, Jul–Sep for quiet; cold and often snowed in Dec–Mar
tip: If you come for the festival, sleep in Artvin and walk up — the single road is closed to traffic and the shuttle queues are long.
todo: Çoruh gorge view from the ridge
rev: The festival is described as loud, chaotic and genuinely local rather than staged; complaints are severe congestion during festival week, almost nothing happening the rest of the year, and litter left behind.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 110 km to Artvin, then 8 km up a steep paved road; taxis run from the town centre

name: Yusufeli and the Çoruh Valley
desc: Be clear about what changed: the 275 m Yusufeli dam closed in 2022 and the reservoir drowned the old town and the classic rafting reach of the Çoruh in 2023. A new town stands on the slope above the water. The side valleys — Barhal, Tekkale, Altıparmak — still run free and are why you come.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the gorge bakes above 35 °C in July–August
tip: Do not plan a Çoruh rafting trip from the old descriptions — what is left is on the Barhal tributary above the reservoir, arranged locally in Yusufeli.
todo: Drive the Barhal valley above the dam
rev: Reactions are mixed and often flat: people who knew the old valley describe the loss bluntly, while first-time visitors still rate the side gorges highly and complain about roadworks, dust and a soulless new town.
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then 170 km north on the rebuilt D950, or Rize–Artvin (RZV) and south via Artvin; buses run from Erzurum and Artvin

name: Barhal Church
desc: A tenth-century Georgian basilica in the village of Altıparmak, high-shouldered, blind-arcaded, and in exceptional condition because it has been in continuous use as the village mosque. The stonework of the east end is the finest in the valley. Kaçkar trailheads start twenty minutes further up the road at Yaylalar.
season: May–Oct; the valley road above Yusufeli is difficult in snow Dec–Mar
tip: Ask at the tea house for the key holder — the interior is normally locked outside prayer times and nobody will offer unless you ask.
todo: Carved east façade of the basilica
Walk on to Yaylalar and Olgunlar
rev: Travellers rate the preservation and the setting, while noting the interior is often locked, there is no interpretation of any kind, and the 30 km valley road from Yusufeli is slow and narrow.
entry: Free — it is a working mosque; dress modestly
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then Yusufeli, then 30 km up the Barhal valley; a dolmuş runs from Yusufeli most days in summer

name: Dörtkilise (Otkhta Eklesia)
desc: A vast tenth-century Georgian monastery church standing roofless in a walnut orchard above Tekkale, far bigger than anything the village around it could ever have needed. Traces of fresco survive high on the apse, and the refectory and chapel ruins are scattered in the trees. Usually you will be the only person there.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the orchard track is muddy after rain and snow closes it in winter
tip: Drive past the village of Tekkale to the very end of the track — most people park at the first ruin, which is the small chapel, and never see the big church.
todo: Nave and apse of the great church
Refectory ruins in the walnut trees
rev: Consistently described as the most impressive and least visited of the Tao-Klarjeti churches, with complaints about the rough unsigned access track, falling masonry, grazing animals inside, and zero facilities.
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then Yusufeli and 7 km up the Tekkale road, then a rough track; taxi from Yusufeli if you have no car

name: İşhan Church
desc: A domed Georgian cathedral on a terrace 1,200 m above the Çoruh, with a carved arcade round the apse that is the best relief carving in the whole Tao-Klarjeti group. Parts of the dome fresco survive. The seven kilometres of hairpins up from the main road are steep, narrow and entirely worth it.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the access road is dangerous in ice and snow
tip: Restoration scaffolding has come and gone here for years — check in Yusufeli whether the interior is currently open before committing to the climb.
todo: Carved blind arcade of the apse
rev: Visitors call the carving world-class and the view extraordinary, while reporting long-running restoration works, scaffolding inside, a locked door on some days, and a nerve-testing single-track road up.
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then the D950 towards Yusufeli and 7 km of hairpins from the İşhan junction; car only

name: Öşkvank (Oshki) Monastery
desc: The largest of the Tao-Klarjeti churches, built in the 960s, with a colonnaded south porch, monumental relief figures of its founders and column capitals carved like Romanesque work three centuries early. It stands in the village of Çamlıyamaç, technically in Erzurum province, but everyone visits it on the Yusufeli church circuit.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the Tortum valley is hot in midsummer and icy in winter
tip: Combine it with İşhan and Tortum waterfall in one day — they are strung along the same road and separately are each a long detour.
todo: Relief figures on the south porch
Combine with İşhan the same day
rev: Described as the most architecturally ambitious church in the region; complaints are decades of stop-start restoration, propped walls, a collapsed section of roof, and modern village building right against the apse.
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then 110 km north on the Tortum–Yusufeli road, turning off at Çamlıyamaç; car or a Yusufeli-based tour

name: Ardanuç and the Cehennem Canyon
desc: The road into Ardanuç threads a limestone slot barely wider than the car, with walls hundreds of metres high and a strip of sky above — locally the Cehennem, hell. Beyond it the valley opens into an orchard basin under the ruined citadel of Gevhernik, the old Georgian Artanuji.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the canyon floor is baking in July–August
tip: Stop in the canyon itself rather than driving straight through — there is one lay-by halfway with room for two cars and it is the only place you can look up properly.
todo: Walk a stretch of the canyon road
Yıldız Tepe viewpoint over the basin
rev: The canyon drive is the part everyone remembers; the complaints are that it lasts only two kilometres, there is nowhere safe to stop, rockfall is frequent, and the town itself has little to detain you.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 110 km to Artvin and 35 km east; minibuses run from Artvin otogar

name: Hopa
desc: The last Turkish town before the Georgian border, a working port of tea warehouses, Laz spoken in the market and lorries queuing for Sarp. It rains here more than anywhere else in the country — over 2,000 mm a year. Come for the border-town texture and the fish, not for beaches.
season: May–Sep; it rains hard in every month and October–December is relentless
tip: Eat hamsi in a harbour lokanta between November and February — outside those months the anchovy on the menu is frozen and everyone local knows it.
todo: Laz market off the main street
Day trip to Sarp and the border
rev: Travellers describe it as scruffy, genuinely lived-in and useful as a base for Borçka and Macahel, while criticising the noise from border traffic, a grey concrete waterfront and near-constant rain.
onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 80 km east on the coast road; buses continue to Batumi through the Sarp crossing

name: Karaca Cave
desc: A dry, warm show cave at 1,550 m above Torul, packed with travertine pools, curtain formations and columns in white and rust-red across a single large chamber. Unlike most Turkish show caves it is properly lit and the walkway is short. The air is claimed to help asthma, which is why half the visitors sit down and stay.
season: Year-round; the access road above Torul can be icy Dec–Mar
tip: It is only about 100 m of walkway — do not build a day around it, but do pair it with Limni lake, which is twenty minutes away.
rev: Rated as one of the better-presented caves in Türkiye, with the consistent caveats that it is small, the visit takes twenty minutes, the stairs from the car park are steep, and it gets crowded with tour buses.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 110 km south over Zigana to Torul, then 17 km up a paved side road

name: Santa Ruins
desc: Seven abandoned Greek hamlets spread across a high forested basin, emptied by the 1923 population exchange and left to the trees. Cut-stone houses with intact door lintels, three ruined churches and a school stand roofless among the beech. Nothing is signed, restored or guarded; you find the villages by following the old paths.
season: Jun–Sep; the track is snowbound Nov–May and impassable in mud after rain
tip: Go with someone who knows the paths, or you will find one hamlet and miss the other six — the churches at Piştovlu and Zurnacılı are the ones to aim for.
todo: Walk between two of the hamlets
rev: People who reach it call it the most haunting place in the region; the complaints are a long rough forest track, no signage or map, treasure-hunter damage everywhere, and collapse that gets worse each year.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 90 km south towards Gümüşhane and a long unsurfaced forest track from Dumanlı; 4x4 or a local guide

name: Tomara Waterfall
desc: Water bursting straight out of a limestone cliff face in a fifty-metre-wide sheet above Şiran — a karst spring rather than a river fall, which is why it runs the same volume in August as in April. Steps and a platform lead to the base, and the spray keeps the whole hollow ten degrees cooler than the plateau.
season: May–Oct; the plateau around is snow-covered and bleak Dec–Mar
tip: This is spring-fed, so unlike almost every other waterfall in the region it is worth visiting in late summer when everything else has dried up.
todo: Platform at the foot of the fall
Walk the terraces above the spring
rev: Visitors are surprised by the width and the volume; the recurring gripes are commercial development right at the base, loud music from the restaurants, weekend crowds and a slippery stair.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 200 km south via Gümüşhane to Şiran, or Erzincan (ERC) from the south; car needed for the last 15 km

name: Limni Lake
desc: A small dark lake at 1,600 m in the pine forest above Torul, with a level path all the way round and a wooden jetty everybody photographs. The water reflects the ridge cleanly on a still morning. In winter it freezes and the forest road becomes a cross-country ski track for the few who know.
season: May–Oct; snow Dec–Mar, when the road is often unploughed
tip: Come up the Zigana side and stop at Torul castle on the way — the lake alone does not justify the drive, the combination does.
todo: Torul castle on the way up
rev: Described as pleasant and quiet rather than spectacular, with complaints about a steep narrow access road, a small car park that fills on weekends, and facilities limited to one café.
entry: ≈₺60 (€1.30) per vehicle at the nature park gate
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 110 km south over Zigana to Torul and 10 km up a forest road

name: Krom Valley
desc: A steep valley of abandoned Greek mining villages north of Gümüşhane, with stone houses stacked on the slopes and several roofless churches still holding their apses. Silver and lead were dug here for centuries; the people left in 1923. Descendants come back most summers and services are occasionally held in the ruins.
season: Jun–Sep; the valley road is impassable with snow Nov–May
tip: Ask in Yağmurdere for the road to Ristbaşı and Kaban — the ruins are strung over fifteen kilometres and there is not a single sign in the valley.
rev: A find for anyone interested in Pontic history, though visitors report the track is rough and long, buildings are collapsing and dug over by treasure hunters, and there is nowhere to eat or sleep in the valley.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 130 km via Gümüşhane and a long mountain road to Yağmurdere; high-clearance vehicle strongly advised

name: Baksı Museum
desc: A contemporary art museum built on a bare ridge above a village 45 km from Bayburt, founded by the artist Hüsamettin Koçan and winner of the Council of Europe Museum Prize in 2014. Modern painting and sculpture sit beside a working collection of local weaving and metalwork, in a building that looks out over empty steppe.
season: May–Oct; the road up is difficult in snow and winter opening is limited
tip: Phone ahead — it keeps short and seasonal hours and people regularly drive 45 km up to a locked door.
rev: Those who get in describe an unexpectedly serious museum in an improbable place; the complaints are erratic opening hours, a long drive on a rough road, and almost no facilities in the village below.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) or Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then to Bayburt and 45 km north on a partly unsurfaced road; car only

name: Bayburt Castle
desc: One of the largest castles in Anatolia, a long walled ridge above the Çoruh with Bagratid foundations and Saltuk and Seljuk rebuilding on top. Restoration has rebuilt long stretches of curtain wall, more heavily than purists like. From the ramparts the whole town and the treeless upland around it lie open.
season: May–Oct; Bayburt is bitterly cold and often snowbound Dec–Mar
tip: Go up at dusk when the walls are floodlit and the town below turns on — daytime light on the bare stone is flat and unrewarding.
rev: Visitors are impressed by the sheer scale and the view and just as often criticise the restoration as over-aggressive concrete work, along with steep uneven paths and little in the way of explanation.
onward: Trabzon (TZX) airport, then 175 km south over Zigana and the Kop pass, or Erzurum (ERZ) and 120 km north; buses run from both

name: Kop Pass
desc: A 2,400 m crossing between Bayburt and Erzurum over treeless upland, with a monument at the summit to the soldiers who froze here in the winter of 1916. There is no forest, no shelter and nothing softening the view — just brown grass, snow poles and weather. A tunnel now takes traffic under the worst of it.
season: Jun–Oct on the old road; snow and closures are routine Nov–May even with the tunnel open
tip: Check the weather before crossing in winter even now — the tunnel helps, but the approaches still close in blizzards and vehicles get stranded.
rev: Drivers describe it as bleak in the best sense and historically affecting; the complaints are severe wind, sudden fog, ice outside high summer, and very little reason to stop beyond the monument.
onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then 80 km north-west on the D915 towards Bayburt; every Erzurum–Trabzon bus crosses it
